# 

# 1\. LAB OVERVIEW

## 1.1  Why This Lab Exists

On AWS the observability building blocks are CloudWatch Logs (log groups and streams, queried with Logs Insights), CloudWatch Metrics (namespaces, dimensions, statistics) and AWS X-Ray (traces, segments and subsegments, now shown in the CloudWatch console under X-Ray traces). AWS Lambda writes every function's output to the log group /aws/lambda/\<function\>, adds a REPORT line with duration, memory and cold-start time to every invocation, publishes Invocations, Errors and Duration metrics, and — with active tracing — sends a trace for each sampled invocation.  
In this lab you deploy a small traced checkout function from a CloudFormation template, send 60 orders with a known mix of results, query its structured JSON logs and REPORT lines with Logs Insights, find cold starts and slow invocations, filter and read X-Ray traces, connect a log line to its trace by trace ID, and confirm what the CloudWatch metrics do and do not count as an error. Everything is done in the AWS Management Console.

| 🎯  NIIT iRUN Alignment |
| :---- |
| INCIDENT OWNERSHIP: You can find failing and slow Lambda invocations and show their trace within minutes. |
|  |
| TROUBLESHOOTING EXCELLENCE: You move from metric to log line to trace using the trace ID instead of guessing. |
|  |
| OPERATIONAL READINESS: You know which failures appear in the Errors metric and which only appear in your logs. |

## 1.3  Conceptual Foundation

One Lambda invocation produces telemetry in three places. The trace ID connects them.  
*Figure: Lambda Telemetry — Invocation → CloudWatch Logs (/aws/lambda/shop-checkout: app JSON lines \+ START/END/REPORT) · X-Ray (AWS::Lambda and AWS::Lambda::Function segments, subsegments inventory and payment) · CloudWatch Metrics (AWS/Lambda Invocations, Errors, Duration, Throttles)*

| Service | What It Holds | Query Tool | Typical Question |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| CloudWatch Logs | Log events per log group and stream | Logs Insights (fields, filter, stats, parse, sort) | Which orders failed, and why? |
| Lambda REPORT line | Duration, Billed Duration, Max Memory, Init Duration, XRAY TraceId | Logs Insights @duration, @initDuration | How slow, how many cold starts? |
| AWS X-Ray | Traces made of segments and subsegments | Filter expressions, trace map, trace details | Where inside the call was time spent? |
| CloudWatch Metrics | Numbers per namespace and dimension | Statistics Sum, Average, Maximum, p95 | How many invocations and errors? |

*Figure: Logs → Trace — App Log Line (trace\_id \= Root of \_X\_AMZN\_TRACE\_ID) and REPORT Line (XRAY TraceId) Carry the Same ID as the X-Ray Trace; Annotations (payment\_result) Make Traces Searchable*

## 1.4  Learning Objectives

* Deploy a Lambda function with active X-Ray tracing and structured JSON logs from a CloudFormation template  
* Query Lambda logs with CloudWatch Logs Insights (fields, filter, stats, sort, parse)  
* Measure duration percentiles and cold starts from REPORT lines  
* Find traces with X-Ray filter expressions and read segments and subsegments  
* Correlate a log line with its trace using the trace ID  
* Explain what the Lambda Invocations, Errors and Duration metrics count

## 1.5  What You Will NOT Do

| 🚫  Hard Stops — Absolute Prohibitions for This Lab |
| :---- |
| ✗  NEVER run this lab in a production AWS account — use a sandbox |
| ✗  NEVER log card numbers, tokens or personal data — log IDs and results only |
| ✗  NEVER add IAM permissions beyond the template — the driver may invoke only your own function |
| ✗  NEVER rely on the Errors metric alone — handled failures (402) are not Lambda errors |
| ✗  NEVER leave the stack behind — delete it at the end (it removes functions, roles and log groups) |

# 3\. CONCEPT DEEP-DIVE BEFORE STARTING

## 3.1  Logs Insights Discovers Fields

CloudWatch Logs Insights queries one or more log groups with a pipeline of commands: fields chooses columns, filter keeps matching events, stats … by aggregates (count(\*), avg(), pct(), max()), sort and limit order the result, and parse extracts fields from text with a glob or a regular expression. When a log event is a JSON object, Logs Insights discovers its keys as fields automatically (level, order\_id, status). For Lambda it also discovers the REPORT line: @type \= "REPORT", @duration, @billedDuration, @maxMemoryUsed and — only on a cold start — @initDuration.

| 💡  Why This Matters Operationally |
| :---- |
| Print one JSON object per event (print(json.dumps(…))) and every field becomes searchable without parse. Python's logging module adds a text prefix by default, which turns the line into plain text — or switch the function's log format to JSON. |
|  |
| Logging the trace ID in every application line is the cheapest way to connect logs and traces: one copy-paste from a log result to the X-Ray console. |

## 3.2  The Critical Distinction: Lambda Errors vs Application Failures

The AWS/Lambda Errors metric counts invocations that ended with an unhandled exception or a timeout. A function that catches a problem and returns statusCode 402 has succeeded as far as Lambda is concerned — the failure exists only in your logs, traces and (if you create one) a custom metric. X-Ray marks segments with fault (server-side, 5xx-like), error (client-side, 4xx-like) or throttle; annotations you add (payment\_result) are indexed so you can filter on them.

| ⚠️  Most Common Mistake With Lambda Observability |
| :---- |
| An engineer looks at the Errors graph, sees 3, and tells support that only 3 orders failed. Support has 9 complaints. |
|  |
| REASON: 6 orders were declined by the payment provider; the function handled them and returned 402, which Lambda counts as a successful invocation. |
|  |
| YOU MUST count failures from the application logs (status, payment\_result) or traces, not only from the Errors metric. |

## 3.3  X-Ray Filter Expressions You Need

| Expression | Finds | Example | Note |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| service("name") | Traces that pass through a service | service("shop-checkout") | Start here |
| fault / error / throttle | Traces with 5xx-like / 4xx-like / 429 flags | fault | Set by AWS or by the SDK |
| responsetime \> n | Traces slower than n seconds | responsetime \> 1 | Whole trace |
| annotation.key \= "v" | Traces with your own indexed values | annotation.payment\_result \= "timeout" | Only annotations, not metadata |

| 📝  How to Decide Between Logs, Traces and Metrics |
| :---- |
| Ask: "Do I need a count, a reason or a location?" Metrics give counts and trends cheaply (how many errors per minute). Logs give the reason per event (which order, which status, which message). Traces give the location of time and failure inside one request (inventory or payment). Start from the metric, use logs to list the affected events, and open the trace of one of them. |

| TASK 2 — LOGS INSIGHTS: Structured Logs, REPORT Lines, Cold Starts |
| :---- |

| 2 | Query the Lambda Logs with CloudWatch Logs Insights*AWS CloudWatch Logs Insights & X-Ray SOP — Day 5 — Lab 1* | ⏱ 8 min |
| :---: | :---- | :---: |

Logs Insights discovers the JSON fields of the application lines and the REPORT fields of every invocation. You list recent events, count by level, break failures down, calculate duration statistics and cold starts, and list the slowest invocations with their X-Ray trace ID parsed from the REPORT line. Run the queries in the console: CloudWatch → Logs → Logs Insights → select the log group /aws/lambda/shop-checkout-\<seat\> → time range 1h → paste the query → Run query.

| ⌨  Task 2 — Logs Insights queries (console) |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Console: CloudWatch → Logs → Logs Insights → Select log group: /aws/lambda/shop-checkout-\<seat\> → time range 1h. Paste ONE query at a time → Run query ![][image21] |
| ![][image22] \# Step 1: recent application events |
| fields @timestamp, level, order\_id, status, payment\_result |
| \| filter ispresent(level) |
| \| sort @timestamp desc |
| \| limit 5 ![][image23]  |
| \# Step 2: events per level, then failures broken down |
| filter ispresent(level) \| stats count(\*) as events by level |
| filter ispresent(level) and level \!= "INFO" \| stats count(\*) as orders by level, status, payment\_result ![][image24] |
| \# Step 3: duration statistics and cold starts from REPORT lines |
| filter @type \= "REPORT" \| stats count(\*) as invocations, avg(@duration) as avg\_ms, pct(@duration, 95\) as p95\_ms, max(@duration) as max\_ms, count(@initDuration) as cold\_starts ![][image25] |
| \# Step 4: slowest invocations with their X-Ray trace ID |
| filter @type \= "REPORT" \| parse @message /XRAY TraceId: (?\<xray\_trace\>\[0-9a-f-\]+)/ \| sort @duration desc \| limit 5 \| fields @requestId, @duration, xray\_trace ![][image26] |
|   **![][image27] 📟  Expected Output** |
| Step 1: 5 rows, e.g. @timestamp=…  level=WARN  order\_id=o-060  status=402  payment\_result=declined |
| Step 2: level=INFO events=51 · level=WARN events=6 · level=ERROR events=3 |
| level=WARN status=402 payment\_result=declined orders=6 · level=ERROR status=504 payment\_result=timeout orders=3 |
| Step 3: invocations=60  avg\_ms≈300–330  p95\_ms≈1240  max\_ms≈1260–1300  cold\_starts=1 (2 if Lambda recycled the environment) |
| Step 4: 4 invocations ≈ 1235–1270 ms (orders 7, 22, 37, 52\) then ≈ 840–870 ms (a timeout); xray\_trace=1-xxxxxxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx |
| **2.A  Record the Step 2 and Step 3 results. Why is @initDuration present on only one or two REPORT lines?**  Answer: Step 2: INFO 51, WARN 6, ERROR 3 (6 declined with status 402, 3 timeouts with 504). Step 3: 60 invocations, p95 about 1.24 s, 1 cold start. @initDuration appears only on the REPORT line of an invocation that started a new execution environment — the first call (and again after Lambda recycles the environment); warm invocations have no initialisation.   |
| **2.B  Why could you filter on level and status without parse, but needed parse for the trace ID in the REPORT line?**  Answer: The application lines are JSON objects, so Logs Insights discovers level, status and order\_id as fields automatically. The REPORT line is plain text from the platform, and the trace ID is only part of that text (XRAY TraceId: …), so it must be extracted with parse and a regular expression.   |

| **3.A  From Step 3: where was the time spent and where did the failure happen? Could you see that in the logs alone?**  Answer: About 800 of the 850 ms were spent in the payment subsegment, which is red (fault); inventory took only 30–60 ms. The log shows that a timeout happened for order o-013 but not how the time was split between inventory and payment — the trace shows the location of time and failure.   |
| **3.B  Why did the annotation filter work, and why would the same value stored as metadata not be searchable?**  Answer: Annotations are indexed by X-Ray, so filter expressions can search them (annotation.payment\_result \= "timeout"). Metadata is stored with the trace but not indexed, so a filter on it finds nothing — use annotations for values you want to search.   |

| **4.A  Errors \= 3 but 9 orders failed. Explain the difference and propose how to make the 6 declined orders visible as a metric.**  Answer: Lambda's Errors metric counts only invocations that end with an unhandled error or timeout (the 3 payment timeouts). The 6 declined orders were handled and returned 402, so Lambda counts them as successful. To make them visible, create a log-based metric (metric filter on status \= 402\) or write the count as an Embedded Metric Format metric from the function, and alarm on it.   |

| **V6: Did you identify where time was spent and where the failure happened?**  Answer: Yes — the payment subsegment took about 800 ms and is marked fault; inventory took about 40 ms.   |

# 

# 6\. TROUBLESHOOTING — COMMON ISSUES & FIXES

| Issue / Error | Cause | Diagnosis | Fix |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Stack creation fails: "already exists" | Function or log group of an earlier attempt with the same seat | CloudFormation → Events tab of the failed stack | Delete the failed stack, delete the old log group /aws/lambda/shop-checkout-\<seat\>, create the stack again |
| Stack creation: insufficient permissions | Sandbox role lacks CloudFormation or IAM rights | Events tab shows the denied action | Ask the instructor for the lab policy (Appendix A) |
| Driver: Task timed out after 3 minutes | Slow account or throttling of invocations | Driver Test result and log | Run the driver again; check Service Quotas → Lambda concurrent executions |
| Logs Insights returns nothing | Wrong log group, region or time range | Log group list: prefix /aws/lambda/shop-checkout | Same region as the stack; last 1 hour; your own seat id |
| X-Ray counts below 60 | Traces still processing, or Lambda sampled fewer requests | Wait 1–2 minutes and run the query again | Re-run; ask the instructor if the count stays below 55 |
| Metrics show no data | Metrics not yet published | Wait 2–3 minutes | Re-run; widen the time range to 3h |

# 7\. INSTRUCTOR DEBRIEF — 7 MINUTES

## 7.1  Discussion Questions

| Discussion 1 — Metric vs Reality |
| :---- |
| Errors \= 3, failed orders \= 9\. Which number belongs on the operations dashboard? |
| How would you create a metric for declined orders (metric filter, Embedded Metric Format)? |
|  |
| Key insight: platform metrics count platform failures; business failures need application metrics from logs or EMF. |
| **Discussion 2 — Cold Starts** |
| How long was your Init Duration, and does it count in @duration? |
| When do cold starts matter for users, and what reduces them? |
|  |
| Key answer: Init Duration is reported separately; it adds to the first request's latency — provisioned concurrency or smaller packages reduce it. |
| **Discussion 3 — Sampling** |
| Why did every invocation get a trace here, and what happens at 100 requests per second? |
| How do you still find the rare failing request when only 5 % are sampled? |
|  |
| Answer: 1 request/s \+ 5 % sampling; at scale, logs (with trace IDs) and metrics find the events, traces explain a sample of them. |
| **Discussion 4 — Annotations vs Metadata** |
| Which values would you add as annotations for an incident search? |
| What must never go into annotations or logs? |
|  |
| Key answer: low-cardinality, searchable values (result, tenant tier, region); never secrets or personal data. |

## 7.2  Common Mistakes — Learn From These

| Mistake | Why It Happens | Consequence | Prevention |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Trusting Errors alone | It is the default graph | Handled failures invisible | Count failures from logs/EMF |
| Text logs with a prefix | logging module defaults | Fields need parse | One JSON object per line or JSON log format |
| No trace ID in logs | Not thought of | Manual correlation | Log the X-Ray Root ID |
| Searching metadata | Values added with put\_metadata | Filter finds nothing | Use annotations for searchable keys |
| Leaving resources | Forgot clean-up | Cost, clutter, security | Delete function, logs, role |

# 8\. EXTENSION TASKS (Advanced Learners)

| Extension A — Log-Based Metric |
| :---- |
| Create a metric filter on the log group (Logs → Log groups → your log group → Metric filters → Create) with the pattern { \$.status \= 402 } and metric DeclinedOrders. |
| Run the driver again (Task 1\) and graph the new metric in CloudWatch → Metrics. |
| Key question: would you alert on it, and at what threshold? Open CloudWatch → Logs → Log groups → select `/aws/lambda/shop-checkout-<seat>`. Open the Metric filters tab → click Create metric filter. Enter the filter pattern: Plaintext `{ $.status = 402 }`  Click Next, assign a custom namespace (e.g., `ShopCheckout`), set Metric name to `DeclinedOrders`, and set Metric value to `1`. Run the driver script from Task 1 again, then go to CloudWatch → Metrics → All metrics → your custom namespace (`ShopCheckout`) to graph `DeclinedOrders`. Answer to Key Question (*Would you alert on it, and at what threshold?*): Yes, on a rate/percentage or anomaly threshold—not on a single occurrence. Why: An HTTP `402` (Payment Required / Declined Card) is a business-level outcome rather than a system crash; individual customers naturally have expired cards or insufficient funds. Alerting on `>= 1` creates constant false-positive alarm fatigue. Recommended Threshold: Alert on a sudden spike or elevated ratio—for example, when `DeclinedOrders / Invocations` exceeds your normal baseline (e.g., greater than 15–20% over a 5–10 minute window), which indicates a broken payment gateway integration, expired API credentials, or a card-testing attack rather than normal user behavior.  |
| **Extension B — JSON Log Format** |
| Set the function log format to JSON (Lambda → Configuration → Monitoring and operations tools → Logging configuration → Edit → Log format JSON). |
| Invoke again and look at the REPORT event — what changed? |
| Adjust the Step 3 query (platform.report fields). Open Lambda → select `shop-checkout-<seat>` → Configuration → Monitoring and operations tools → Logging configuration → Edit. Change Log format from `Text` to JSON and save. Invoke the function again and inspect the log stream in CloudWatch Logs. What Changed in the `REPORT` Event: Instead of an unstructured plain-text line (`REPORT RequestId: ... Duration: 12.34 ms Billed Duration: 13 ms Memory Size: 128 MB Max Memory Used: 65 MB`), Lambda emits a structured JSON object with `"type": "platform.report"` and nested metrics inside a `record` object (`record.metrics.durationMs`, `record.metrics.billedDurationMs`, `record.metrics.memorySizeMB`, `record.metrics.maxMemoryUsedMB`, and `record.requestId`). Because it is native JSON, CloudWatch Logs Insights automatically discovers all fields without needing regex `parse` commands. filter type \= "platform.report" \| stats count(\*) as invocations,         avg(record.metrics.durationMs) as avg\_ms,         pct(record.metrics.durationMs, 95\) as p95\_ms,         max(record.metrics.maxMemoryUsedMB) as max\_mem\_mb  |
| **Extension C — Application Signals** |
| Read about CloudWatch Application Signals and Transaction Search. |
| How do they relate to X-Ray traces and OpenTelemetry? |
| Which would you use for a new service? **OpenTelemetry (OTel):** The vendor-neutral instrumentation standard (SDKs and AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry / ADOT) used to emit traces, metrics, and logs from your application code. **X-Ray Traces & Transaction Search:** X-Ray is AWS's distributed tracing backend. Traditionally, X-Ray sampled a small percentage of requests (e.g., 5%) to control costs. **CloudWatch Transaction Search** allows you to ingest **100% of trace spans** directly into CloudWatch Logs at lower cost, letting you search high-cardinality attributes (like `order_id` or `customer_id`) across every single request without sampling gaps. **CloudWatch Application Signals:** AWS's zero-code/auto-instrumented APM layer built directly on top of OpenTelemetry and X-Ray. It automatically discovers services, builds service topology maps, and tracks golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, faults) and SLOs without requiring custom metric filters or manual dashboards. **Which Would You Use for a New Service?** Use **CloudWatch Application Signals** (instrumented via **OpenTelemetry**) paired with **Transaction Search** enabled. **Why:** You get out-of-the-box RED metrics (Rate, Errors, Duration), dependency maps, and SLO tracking with zero custom metric code, while OpenTelemetry avoids vendor lock-in and Transaction Search ensures you never miss an intermittent failure due to trace sampling.  |

# 10\. QUICK REFERENCE — AWS LOGS INSIGHTS & X-RAY COMMAND CARD

Bookmark this page. Every command you need in SOP order.

| Category | Command | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Choose fields | fields @timestamp, level, order\_id | Columns |
| Filter | filter level \= "ERROR" and status \>= 500 | Rows |
| Aggregate | stats count(\*) by level, bin(1m) | Counts |
| Percentile | stats pct(@duration, 95\) | Latency |
| Cold starts | filter @type \= "REPORT" \| stats count(@initDuration) | Init |
| Parse text | parse @message /XRAY TraceId: (?\<t\>\[0-9a-f-\]+)/ | Extract |
| Field exists | filter ispresent(level) | JSON lines only |
| X-Ray service | service("shop-checkout-u07") | Filter |
| X-Ray flags | fault · error · throttle | Filter |
| X-Ray latency | responsetime \> 1 | Filter (s) |
| X-Ray annotation | annotation.payment\_result \= "timeout" | Filter |
| Lambda metrics | AWS/Lambda Invocations · Errors · Duration · Throttles | Metrics |

# APPENDIX A — INSTRUCTOR PRE-CLASS RUNBOOK (INSTRUCTOR ONLY)

INSTRUCTOR ONLY — nothing in this lab needs a command line for the learners; the instructor prepares the account once.  
1\. Account and region: one sandbox AWS account (never production) in one region for the whole cohort. Check Service Quotas → Lambda → Concurrent executions: every learner uses at most 2 concurrent executions (driver \+ function), so 40 learners need at least 80; new accounts often start at 10 — request an increase two days before class or split the cohort over two accounts.  
2\. Learner access: give each learner a console sign-in (IAM Identity Center or IAM users) with the sandbox policy in the kit (aws/instructor/learner-sandbox-policy.json: CloudFormation, Lambda, IAM roles named shop-lab\*, CloudWatch Logs, X-Ray and CloudWatch read access). Review it in your account before class — it has not been tested in your organisation.  
3\. Template check (once, before class): create the stack with seat u00, run the driver, run the five filter expressions and the Logs Insights queries, then delete the stack. Expected: 60 / 3 / 4 / 6 traces, INFO 51 · WARN 6 · ERROR 3\. If the X-Ray subsegments (inventory, payment) do not appear, only the Lambda service segments are shown — the lab then still teaches logs, REPORT lines and trace IDs, and the custom subsegments and annotations (Task 3 Steps 1 and 3\) fall back to the Lambda segments; tell learners to skip the annotation filters.  
4\. Sampling: Lambda samples the first request each second and 5 % of the rest, per function; the driver sends one order per second, so every order should be traced. If a cohort-wide shared sampling rule is set up in your account, check the counts in step 3\.  
5\. No CloudFormation access? Learners create the two Lambda functions by hand: Lambda → Create function → Author from scratch (Python 3.13) → paste shop-checkout-app.py / shop-order-driver.py from the kit → Configuration → Monitoring: enable Active tracing → driver: Timeout 3 min, environment variable TARGET \= the checkout function name, and an inline policy allowing lambda:InvokeFunction on that function only. Allow 15 more minutes.  
6\. Clean-up: every learner deletes the stack (Task 4 Step 3). After class search CloudFormation for stacks named shop-lab1-\* and delete the rest; the 1-day log retention removes stray log groups within a day.
